idiom_name: owning handle struct + release function, bound to scope with __attribute__((cleanup))
implementation_notes: C has no destructors and no ownership in the type system, so the whole structure is hand-written: a handle struct carries the pointee and its release operation, a creation function returns the handle with ownership transferred to the caller, and a drop function releases exactly once. What replaces the compiler's automatic destruction is a calling convention plus, where GNU/Clang extensions are available, __attribute__((cleanup(fn))) on the handle variable so release runs when the variable leaves scope. Counting, when ownership is shared, is added by hand (kernel kref or GLib GObject style; see intrusive-reference-counting) and every exit path must call the release. CPython's PyObject protocol - Py_INCREF/Py_DECREF with documented strong and borrowed reference rules - is the reference example of this convention in production C.
pitfalls: The cleanup function also runs when control jumps past the variable's initialisation (goto, early switch), so it must tolerate an uninitialised or NULL handle.
Ownership is a convention only: copying the handle struct aliases the same pointer and two drops double-free, and nothing in the type prevents it.
Any exit path that bypasses the scope hook leaks and only ASan/valgrind will notice; there is no runtime safety net.
A shared handle needs an atomic count plus acquire/release ordering before the final free, or concurrent drops race.
